text: Reading Father McBrien’s autobiographical sketch, one is struck by the two major concerns of his life: politics and his own career. “I am a theologian today only because I am a priest,” he writes, and he is a priest because he had “been oriented from the earliest years of my conscious existence to the Catholic priesthood.” Born.and raised in Hartford, Con- necticut, as the son of an Irish policeman and an Italian mother who was a registered nurse, McBrien describes his own childhood as “ordinary,” the only unusual thing about it being his “early preoccupation with politics.” He clearly remembers the election of 1948, being 12 at the time, as well as the Eisenhower-Stevenson race in 1952. “Thereafter,” he writes, “the political process itself became an object of consuming attention, with my range of study gradually broadening from absorption with electoral politics to a con- centration on more fundamental questions of philosophy.” Given his own personal preoccupation with politics and the social encouragement he evidently experienced to be- come a priest, it is only logical that the two should lead him to aninterest in ecclesiology, which he saw as the application of political insights to the structure of the Church.
